Doha Defies The Odds

blocks.caption: Joe Russo Getty Images for Doha Film Festival

blocks.text: Raft of heavy hitters: Qatar’s Doha Film Festival closes this evening after a second successful edition in its revamped format, having defied the complicated regional geopolitical tensions in the backdrop sparked by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. The mood around Doha’s Katara Cultural Village, which hosted the festival, and other hotspots like the Msheireb Downtown district and adjacent Souq Wafiq, was generally relaxed, with restaurants and other venues packed out. Big names passing through included James Gray with Paper Tiger , while Japanese Cannes regular Naomi Kawase was jury president. Program highlights included Sara Isaq’s opening film, The Station, set in a female-only gas station in a remote part of Yemen and giving a rare human insight into a country too long associated with conflict. As well as Ishaq and her scattered cast, the festival flew in several Yemeni figures such as Yemeni-U.S. coffee entrepreneur Mokhtar Alkhanshali, the subject of Dave Eggers Monk of Mokha, and influencer Nadir Nahdi. There were also strong Palestinian and Gulf region delegations. The Station is among 15 films in international competition and you can keep an eye on Deadline for the winners later this evening. The festival also hosted the second edition of the Film Committee at Media City Qatar’s Industry Days from November 19 to 21, which saw a raft of industry heavy-hitters stop by to discuss the region’s burgeoning film and TV sectors along with Joe Russo (pictured) and a very special Avengers trailer . Read all about it here .

blocks.text: Tricky Week For BAFTA
Watch on Deadline

It’s Bad, It’s Bad (You Know It): A tricky week for BAFTA as it nervously prepares for the first Film Awards since the car-crash I Swear saga. It was reported over the weekend that the team behind one of the year’s biggest Box Office success stories, Michael Jackson biopic Michael, will not be submitting the Antoine Fuqua movie for consideration. At this point, motivations are unclear, but GK Films producer Graham King criticized the awards body plus BBC after the I Swear saga for “displaying cultural insensitivity and tone deafness.” This may have contributed to GK’s decision to wrench Michael away from the BAFTAs. There is also the fact that the Leaving Neverland documentary , which spotlighted two men alleging the deceased singer groomed then sexually abused them, won a TV BAFTA several years back. Either way, this was unwelcome news with the event less than three months away. Compounding the Michael reports was BAFTA losing its longtime headline film awards sponsor , EE. This decision was driven by EE’s “business strategy,” according to the awards org, but the timing could have been better. Nerves will be jangling at BAFTA’s Piccadilly HQ and executives will be looking to avoid any more of these stories before the curtain rises in late Feb.

Global Breakout: ‘Saint-Pierre’

You’d be forgiven for being unfamiliar with the French-controlled territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, but Canadian audiences will be more than aware now they have digested Alan Hawco’s hit procedural Saint-Pierre, which was our Global Breakout this week. Hawco, who also produces, took us behind the scenes of the making of a show that proves small island life can provide all the drama. For Hawco, a U.S. deal is surely close. >>> Read The Breakout

The Essentials
🌶️ Hot One : Wild Horse Nine producer Blueprint Pictures has taken English-language remake rights to German dramedy No Hit Wonder .
🌶️ Another : Netflix is making its first wildlife film out of Latin America with the Fernanda Torres-narrated March of the Jaguars.
🌶️ Yet another : Documentarian Sarah Macdonald and a leading women’s rights lawyer are investigating allegations among the waves in The Dark Side Of Surfing .
🕯️ Paying tribute: With a little help from Helena Bonham Carter, Baz paid tribute to legendary British agent Jeremy Conway.
✍️ Investigation: SkyShowtime staff complained about workplace culture and the handling of alleged “racist conduct” by an unnamed manager before the streamer was given the chop.
📖 Analysis: The British industry has been spooked by the proposed U.S. federal film and TV tax credit. It is quietly taking action.
🏆 Awards latest: France’s Caréme was the big winner at the David Zaslav and Bela Bajaria-attended International Emmys.
🏪 Setting up shop: Veteran entertainment execs including former UTA staffer Sam Glynne set up The Unlabelled Alliance.
🤝 Done deal: Amazon MGM Studios has inked an overall deal with Ullisses Campbell, the award-winning Brazilian journalist and crime writer.
⛺ Fest latest: The Rotterdam Film Festival has its next MD, Pepijn Kuyper, who succeeds Clare Stewart.
🍿 Box office: Focker-In-Law and Hexed are eying worldwide five-day openings of $70M and $75M respectively.
🎥 Trailer: For Bunker , Florian Zeller’s Venice breakout with Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem.
